reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO / India NTEP
clinicalPearls: A sexually transmitted infection caused by the invasive L1-L3 serovars of Chlamydia trachomatis, distinct from the serovars causing ordinary genital chlamydia
Classically progresses through a primary transient painless genital ulcer or papule, a secondary stage of painful inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes), and a late destructive fibrotic stage
The 'groove sign', where enlarged nodes straddle the inguinal ligament, is a characteristic secondary-stage finding
In men who have sex with men, LGV commonly presents as a severe haemorrhagic proctocolitis that can mimic inflammatory bowel disease
Untreated late disease causes lymphatic obstruction with genital elephantiasis, strictures and fistulae
Diagnosis rests on detecting Chlamydia trachomatis by nucleic acid amplification with genotyping to identify LGV serovars, alongside serology in some settings
Treatment is a prolonged course of doxycycline as the preferred agent, with buboes aspirated rather than incised, and partners evaluated and treated
reference.pathophysiology: The L-serovars of Chlamydia trachomatis are more invasive than the ocular and genital serovars and preferentially infect macrophages and lymphatic tissue. After inoculation at a mucosal site, the organism spreads to draining lymph nodes, provoking a granulomatous and suppurative lymphadenitis with stellate abscesses. Persistent inflammation leads to lymphatic obstruction, fibrosis and tissue destruction in the chronic stage. Rectal inoculation produces an intense proctocolitis with ulceration and, if untreated, strictures and fistulae.
additionalInvestigations: Nucleic acid amplification testing for Chlamydia trachomatis from ulcer, rectal or bubo aspirate specimens
Chlamydia serology as supportive evidence in some settings
Screening for HIV, syphilis and other sexually transmitted infections
Sigmoidoscopy with biopsy when proctocolitis mimics inflammatory bowel disease
redFlags: Severe proctocolitis with bleeding and pain, especially in HIV-positive men who have sex with men
Fluctuant buboes at risk of rupture requiring aspiration
Late fibrotic complications such as genital elephantiasis, strictures or fistulae
Coexisting HIV infection altering severity and management
reference.prognosis: Early treatment gives complete recovery, but delayed diagnosis allows irreversible lymphatic damage with strictures, fistulae and genital lymphoedema; extended antibiotic courses may be needed in advanced or HIV-associated disease.
pitfalls: Mistaking LGV proctocolitis for inflammatory bowel disease and delaying antibiotics
Using a standard short chlamydia course rather than the extended regimen LGV requires
Incising buboes instead of aspirating, risking chronic sinus formation
Failing to genotype and thus missing invasive LGV serovars
management: Extended-course oral doxycycline as first-line antimicrobial therapy, with erythromycin or azithromycin as alternatives (for example in pregnancy)
Aspiration of fluctuant buboes to relieve symptoms and prevent rupture, avoiding incision where possible
Prolonged antibiotic courses for late-stage or HIV-associated disease
Screen for and treat concurrent HIV, syphilis and other sexually transmitted infections
Notify, test and empirically treat recent sexual partners
Surgical management of late complications such as strictures, fistulae and genital lymphoedema
Refer to genitourinary or sexual health services for treatment and contact tracing
